_about: Scam watch: real phishing emails Unmask analysed, newest first. Only real cases from public research collections or user reports that the reporter agreed to publish. Every address is defanged. Add an entry with a pull request; see CONTRIBUTING.md.

items.title: A fake COLDCARD "security advisory"
items.lure: Owners are told to book a "10-minute call" through a link to collect a refund.
tells: The sender domain only contains the brand name: coldcardblog[.]org is not COLDCARD's.
The booking link goes to another look-alike, book.coinkiteadvisory[.]com.
It passes DMARC, because the scammers own the look-alike domain. Passing proves who sent it, not that it is safe.
items.lesson: A brand name inside a domain doesn't make it the brand's domain. Go to the company's site yourself.

items.title: A fake Binance "withdrawal successful" email
items.lure: It announces a withdrawal you didn't make and offers a "Cancel this transaction" button.
tells: It is sent from auswestbc[.]com[.]au, not from Binance, yet shows Binance's real logo.
It was sent by a script (PHPMailer), not by a company mail system.
The whole email is one clickable picture, so spam filters can't read it.
items.lesson: Panic is the lure. Open the app or site yourself instead of clicking "Cancel" in an email.

items.title: A fake Efteling gift-card survey
items.lure: A gift card for "confirming your participation" in a survey.
tells: A link shows www.efteling.com but really goes to another website.
The sender name is written in look-alike mathematical letters to dodge filters.
41 tracking pixels report when and where it is opened.
items.lesson: Free gift cards for a quick survey are almost always bait. Check where the link really goes.
